## About

Attorney, accountant and university lecturer. Doctoral candidate in Law at IDP, Brazil,
since 2026. This site gathers what I write and what I read in tax law, white-collar
crime and corporate law, with particular attention to the use of artificial
intelligence in legal research.

The Portuguese version carries the full contents, including all articles, notes and
reading files. This page summarises the research line for readers outside Brazil.

## The research problem

Methodological literature prescribes reproducibility for empirical research assisted
by large language models: open-weight models, self-hosting, pinned versions, declared
parameters, and verification of the same prompt across several models. The empirical
literature that classifies legal text at scale meets little of that prescription, for
reasons of feasibility, so that the two bodies of work seldom intersect.

## The claim

**I argue that reproducibility is a measurable property of each variable of the
instrument, to be measured and reported field by field.**

I call this *functional replicability by field*. A single study may be fully
replicable in some variables while failing in others, so that a blanket statement
about a study being reproducible says little about what can actually be reused.

The supporting evidence is my own. On the same corpus, with the same model, on the
same day, agreement between automated classification and human adjudication ranged
from **0.97 in one field to 0.17 in another**, and only four of ten fields met the
adopted acceptance criterion. I publish the lowest figure alongside the highest,
because the value of the measure lies in showing where the instrument fails.

## The gap

A systematic review of the literature, recording a verbatim excerpt and source page
for every mention, found no study that submits the same legal protocol, in
Portuguese, to a panel of both open and proprietary models with formal measurement of
stability. Each of the nearest works falls short of one of those three conditions.
